text: Tamsin Arts Centre is the home of the Asterford University Drama Society, which stages a large production in its main theatre every spring. The centre also hosts touring orchestras, comedy nights and a festival of short films made by students, and its cafe is a popular meeting place in the evenings.

Recycling bins for paper, glass, plastic and food waste are placed throughout the campus. Food waste from Juniper Refectory is turned into compost for the university gardens, and a student-run swap shop collects unwanted furniture and kitchen equipment at the end of each year for reuse by new students.

The Ferryman is the oldest inn in Asterford and stands beside the river near the old stone bridge. Its low beams and open fireplace attract students and residents alike, and a quiz night held every Tuesday is often won by teams of lecturers from the history and physics departments.

Each summer Asterford University runs a summer school for secondary school pupils from across the region. Participants stay in the residences for a week, attend lectures and workshops in subjects they are considering for university, and finish with a presentation of a group project to their families.

The Poetry Circle meets in a quiet corner of the Green Kettle cafe to share new poems and discuss the work of established writers. Members publish a small printed anthology each year, and the circle invites poets from across the region to read their work at an evening event in the spring.

The university football club runs several men's and women's teams that compete in regional student leagues. Training takes place on floodlit pitches near the sports centre, and the club also organises a friendly five-a-side tournament each term that is open to any student who can form a team.

Pellam Observatory was designed by the architect Corwin Bastable, who was known for buildings that combined scientific function with careful decoration. Bastable placed the telescope dome on a heavy stone tower so that passing carts and strong winds would not shake the instruments, and he added a small library and a lecture room at the base of the tower.

Hollin Library is the main library of Asterford University. After its last refurbishment it offers 640 study seats spread across silent reading rooms, group study areas and a long gallery overlooking the quadrangle. During the examination period almost every one of these seats is taken by mid-morning, and students often arrive before the doors open to secure a place.

Tamsin Arts Centre opened in 1971 and is named after Tamsin Vale, an actress born in Asterford who left her savings to support theatre in the town. The centre contains a main theatre with 420 seats, a studio theatre, a cinema screen and a gallery for exhibitions of student art.

Brindle Hall was built in 1962 from red brick and has four floors arranged around a central courtyard. Its warden is Dr. Felix Amory, a lecturer in philosophy who lives in a flat on the ground floor and organises regular dinners for residents in the hall's panelled dining room.

The university keeps several beehives on the roof of the biology building, looked after by students and a member of staff who is an experienced beekeeper. The honey is sold in small jars at the campus shop, and the hives are used to study how bees use the flowers of the gardens and the surrounding countryside.

The Wend Water Festival takes place in Asterford every summer and celebrates the river that gave the town its prosperity. Highlights include a raft race between local businesses, a parade of decorated boats and a fireworks display over the water on the final night.

The town bus service in Asterford is run by a small local company and connects the market square with the outlying villages of the valley. Buses are less frequent in the evenings and on Sundays, so students living outside the town often share lifts or cycle instead.

Safety rules in the Sable Chemistry Laboratory require all students to wear goggles and closed shoes, and food and drink are never allowed inside the teaching rooms. Fire blankets, eye-wash stations and emergency showers are placed near every exit, and a fire drill is held at the start of each term.

The University Museum displays objects collected by staff and students since the foundation of Asterford University, including fossils, scientific instruments, coins and pottery from local excavations. It is free to visit, and school groups from the region come regularly for guided tours led by student volunteers.

In the 1960s Asterford University expanded rapidly, adding new science buildings, residences and a sports centre on land that had previously been farmland. Student numbers more than doubled within a decade, and many of the modern concrete buildings on the northern side of the campus date from this period.

Brindle Hall stands on Larch Lane, a quiet street lined with lime trees about ten minutes' walk from the centre of the campus. The hall has a bicycle shed, a laundry room and a small gym in the basement, and the Campus Loop shuttle stops at the end of the lane.

A towpath runs along the River Wend from the edge of Asterford to the village of Millbrook, about six kilometres downstream. It is a favourite route for joggers and dog walkers, and in spring the banks are covered with wild garlic and bluebells.

Aster Archive opens at 09:00 on weekdays, when the porter unlocks the heavy oak doors on Chancel Street and the first readers collect their reserved boxes from the issue desk. Researchers who plan a long day in the archive often arrive a few minutes early, because the most popular desks by the tall windows are quickly taken.

The first librarian of Hollin Library was Agatha Wrenfield, who was appointed when the building opened and held the post for nearly thirty years. She introduced the card catalogue, persuaded wealthy families in the town to donate their private collections, and insisted that the reading rooms remain open to townspeople as well as students.

Asterford University Press publishes academic books, journals and a series of guides to the history and landscape of the region. Its offices are in a former printing works on Tanner Street, and an old hand press is still kept in working order to print invitations for special university events.

The Student Health Centre of Asterford University is housed in Fenwick Lodge, a former gatekeeper's house at the southern entrance of the campus. The lodge was later extended with a single-storey wing that now contains consulting rooms, a small pharmacy counter and a quiet waiting area with views of the gardens.

Before the present head took over, the Department of Maritime History was led for many years by Professor Alfred Toller, who retired in 2015. Toller was known for his studies of lighthouse keepers and coastal smuggling, and a seminar room in the department is now named in his honour.

A bicycle hire scheme operates across the Asterford University campus, with docking stations outside the main library, the science buildings and the residences. Students can rent a bicycle for a small annual fee, and the scheme is popular because the campus is spread across several hills.

Asterford University has installed solar panels on the roofs of many of its buildings and heats several residences using a wood-chip boiler supplied from local forests. The university aims to reduce its carbon emissions to zero within the next two decades, and students take part through an energy-saving competition between residences.

The Accommodation Office manages the residences of Asterford University and helps students find rooms in private houses in the town. It keeps a register of approved landlords, inspects shared houses for safety, and offers advice when disputes arise between tenants and landlords.

The Founders' Lantern Walk begins at the gates of Hollin Library, where the vice-chancellor lights the first lantern and gives a short speech about the history of Asterford University. The walkers then cross the old stone bridge over the River Wend and climb slowly through the narrow streets of the old town.

The Robotics Club brings together students from engineering, computer science and physics who build small robots for national competitions. Its workshop is crowded with circuit boards, motors and spare wheels, and the club's line-following robot once won a regional prize against teams from much larger universities.

About 38 researchers work at the Marrow Physics Laboratory, including permanent staff scientists, postdoctoral fellows and doctoral students. The group is known across Asterford University for its work on superconducting materials, and its members meet every Thursday afternoon to present results and discuss problems with their experiments.

Research at Asterford University is funded by government councils, charities and partnerships with industry. Some of its best-known work concerns river ecology, rural health and the history of the wool trade, reflecting the close links between the university and its surrounding valley.

During the examination period Hollin Library stays open day and night, and a security officer patrols the reading rooms after midnight. The library cafe on the ground floor serves coffee, soup and sandwiches until late in the evening, and students are allowed to bring covered drinks into most of the study areas.

Cross-country running has a long history at Asterford University, where the hills provide ideal courses across muddy fields and steep paths. The club's annual race to the summit of Beacon Hill and back is a test of endurance that attracts runners from the town as well as students.

The main telescope of Pellam Observatory has a mirror with a diameter of 1.2 metres. The mirror was cast and polished in a specialist workshop and carried up the hill on a reinforced cart, and it remains the largest telescope mirror owned by Asterford University. Researchers use it mainly to measure the brightness of variable stars.

Hollin Library holds about 1.1 million printed volumes, together with a large collection of journals, newspapers and music scores. Its collections are spread over several floors, and the rare books are kept in a locked room on the top floor where they can be read only under the supervision of a librarian.

The Department of Earth Sciences is housed in a stone building on the northern edge of the campus, close to the observatory hill. Its corridors display rock samples and fossils collected in the Brannock Hills, and its students study volcanoes, earthquakes, climate and the history of the planet.

Professor Desmond Achterberg is the editor of the Asterford Review of Economic History, a journal published twice a year by the university press. He also chairs the committee that awards travel grants to doctoral students who need to visit archives in other countries.

Kestrel Boathouse stands on the bank of the River Wend just below the old stone bridge and was opened in 1934. It is the home of the Asterford University Boat Club, whose members train on the river early in the morning before lectures begin.

Asterford University has exchange agreements with partner universities in many countries, allowing students to spend a term or a full year studying abroad. In return, exchange students from those universities come to Asterford each year and often join the International Students Society.

Aster Archive is built of pale grey limestone and has a slender clock tower above its main entrance. Inside, the Long Room serves as the reading room, with twenty-four desks under a painted ceiling, while the strong rooms below hold charters, letters, maps and account books belonging to Asterford University and the town.

The Asterford Town Museum occupies a former wool warehouse beside the river and tells the story of the town from its earliest settlement to the present day. Its displays include a reconstructed weaver's cottage, tools from the old mills and a collection of shop signs from the market square.

A farmers' market is held in the courtyard of the Corn Exchange on the first Saturday of each month. Local producers sell meat, eggs, honey, apple juice and the famous Brannock blue cheese, and the market is a popular place for students to buy food produced within a few miles of the town.

Professor Orla Penhaligon grew up in the small fishing village of Porthwenna and studied geography before turning to research. She is a popular public speaker, and her evening talks at Tamsin Arts Centre about life at polar field camps regularly fill the main theatre.

The Founders' Lantern Walk is an annual procession held in October at Asterford University. On the chosen evening, students, staff and townspeople carry paper lanterns through the streets of the old town to remember the founding of the university, and many local shops stay open late to serve warm drinks to the walkers.

Asterford University has about nine thousand five hundred students, of whom roughly a fifth are postgraduates. Around one in eight students comes from abroad, and the university employs about two thousand staff, making it by far the largest employer in the town.

The campus print shop prints posters, theses and course booklets for students and staff at reasonable prices. It is especially busy at the end of the academic year when final-year students submit their dissertations, and staff often work late into the evening to meet deadlines.

Pellam Observatory holds public viewing nights on Friday evenings when the sky is clear. Visitors climb the spiral staircase to the dome, where student volunteers point the smaller refracting telescope at the Moon, the planets and bright star clusters, and explain what can be seen through the eyepiece.

Sports Day at Asterford University is held at the end of the summer term and brings together the residences in a series of light-hearted competitions. Events include a sack race, a tug of war and a relay around the main lawn, and the winning residence receives a silver cup that has been awarded since the early twentieth century.

The Astronomy Society of Asterford University organises talks, stargazing trips into the dark countryside of the Brannock Hills and workshops on photographing the night sky. Members bring their own binoculars or small telescopes, and the society lends equipment to beginners who do not have any.

The Campus Loop shuttle has eight stops, including the Student Union, the science buildings, Brindle Hall and the market square. On weekdays the first bus leaves at 07:00 and the last one returns to its depot at 23:00, and drivers announce each stop in advance.

The Climbing Club trains on an indoor wall at the Ridgeway Sports Centre during the week and travels to the limestone crags of the Brannock Hills at weekends. Safety training is given to every new member, and experienced climbers lead beginners on easy routes until they gain confidence.

The University Choir sings at formal ceremonies, at concerts in St Brannoc's Church and at the end of the Founders' Lantern Walk. New members join after a short audition at the start of the year, and the choir travels each summer to perform at a music festival in another town.

Student radio at Asterford University broadcasts from a small studio in the basement of the Student Union. Volunteer presenters host shows on music, sport, science and politics, and the station is best known for its live coverage of election nights and the annual debate between student candidates.

The Asterford University Chess Club meets twice a week in a seminar room of the Student Union and welcomes players of every level. Members compete in a regional league against teams from other universities and towns, and the club holds a lightning tournament at the end of each term with a small trophy for the winner.

Asterford University is organised into five faculties, which cover the arts and humanities, the social sciences, the natural sciences, engineering, and medicine and health. Each faculty is led by a dean, and the faculties are further divided into departments responsible for teaching and research in particular subjects.

The Department of Maritime History owns a collection of 114 model ships, many of them built by sailors during long voyages. The models are displayed in glass cabinets along the main corridor, and students on the museum studies course help to clean, catalogue and photograph them each summer.

Aster Archive is the historic archive building of Asterford University and stands on Chancel Street in the old part of the campus. On weekdays the archive closes at 18:00, and staff ask readers to return all boxes to the issue desk a quarter of an hour before closing. Evening research groups therefore usually meet in Hollin Library instead.

The Language Centre offers evening classes in more than a dozen languages for students, staff and members of the public. Courses range from complete beginner to advanced conversation, and the centre also provides English language support for international students who want to improve their academic writing.

Open days for prospective students are held at Asterford University several times a year. Visitors can attend sample lectures, tour the residences and talk to current students and staff, and a free minibus carries families between the main campus and the sports facilities on the hillside.

Professor Orla Penhaligon teaches glaciology at Asterford University. Her lectures explain how glaciers form, move and retreat, and she regularly brings ice cores from her field work into the classroom so that students can see the layers of ancient snow for themselves. Her course is one of the most popular options in the Department of Earth Sciences.

Asterford University was founded in 1842 by a charter granted to a small college of teachers who had been giving public lectures in the town hall. For its first decades the university taught only theology, classics and natural philosophy, and it had fewer than one hundred students, most of them sons of local farmers and merchants.

The Student Union cafe is one of the busiest places on campus between lectures, offering coffee, tea, toasted sandwiches and soup at prices kept low for students. Large windows look out over the market square, and the cafe's notice board is covered with advertisements for rooms, concerts and club meetings.

The Marrow Physics Laboratory opened in 1931 and is named after Helena Marrow, a physicist who studied the behaviour of metals at very low temperatures. Her notebooks and some of her original apparatus are displayed in a glass case near the laboratory entrance, alongside a photograph of the first research group.

The IT help desk is located in the main teaching building and assists students and staff with problems involving passwords, wireless access, printing and university software. Most questions are answered on the spot, and the help desk lends laptops to students whose own computers are being repaired.

Asterford Town Hall stands on the south side of the market square and was built in the eighteenth century from the same honey-coloured stone as many of the older houses. The town council meets in its upper chamber, and the ground floor is used for exhibitions, concerts and wedding ceremonies.

A small pond in the Varden Gardens is home to a pair of swans, several families of ducks and a population of frogs that students study in biology classes. The swans have become unofficial mascots of the university, and their cygnets are watched closely by students each spring.

The Winter Book Fair takes place in December, shortly before the end of the autumn term, and is one of the busiest events in the Asterford calendar. Many visitors combine a trip to the fair with the Christmas market held in the market square on the same weekend.

The university jazz band plays at the Student Union bar on Friday nights and at many college dinners. It began as a small group of friends playing in a practice room and now includes a full brass section, a singer and a rhythm section, and its members often go on to play in professional bands.

A total of 26 boats are stored in Kestrel Boathouse, ranging from single sculls to long racing shells for eight rowers. The boats rest on tall wooden racks along both walls, and each one carries the name of a former club captain painted in small silver letters on its bow.

On Saturdays the Student Health Centre at Asterford University opens at 08:30 and offers a short morning session for urgent appointments and repeat prescriptions. The Saturday session is staffed by one doctor and two nurses, and students who feel unwell over the weekend are encouraged to arrive early because places are limited.

The ruins of Asterford Castle stand on a rocky hill above the town and are reached by a steep path from the market square. Only parts of the outer walls and a single round tower survive, but the site offers wide views over the valley and is a popular place for students to watch the sunset.

The Department of Philosophy is housed in a row of tall terraced houses on Chancel Street that the university bought at the beginning of the twentieth century. Its seminar rooms still have fireplaces and wooden shutters, and the department is known for its research on ethics and the philosophy of mind.

In earlier centuries Asterford grew wealthy from the wool trade, as sheep grazed on the Brannock Hills and the wool was washed and spun in mills along the river. Many of the grand houses in the town were built by wool merchants, and a sheep still appears on the town's coat of arms.

The box office of Tamsin Arts Centre closes at 20:00 on most days, although it stays open until the start of the performance on evenings when there is a show. Tickets can also be reserved by telephone, and reserved tickets are kept at the counter until shortly before curtain-up.

The River Wend flows through the centre of Asterford from the hills in the north towards the sea. In past centuries it powered more than a dozen mills, and today it is used mainly for rowing, fishing and boat trips, while a footpath follows its banks for many kilometres in both directions.

A tall bell tower rises above the Great Court of Asterford University and marks the hours with a deep chime that can be heard across the town. The bell was cast from metal donated by local families and bears an inscription in Latin praising learning and service.

Rooms in Brindle Hall are allocated mainly to first-year students, although a small number of places are kept for international postgraduates. Each spring the residents organise the Brindle Hall garden party in the courtyard, with music, food stalls and a croquet match against the neighbouring hall.

The Debating Society of Asterford University is one of the oldest student societies and holds formal debates in the Varden Lecture Theatre. Guest speakers are invited to argue for or against a motion, and the audience votes at the end of each evening by leaving the room through one of two doors.

A children's reading corner is one of the most popular features of the Winter Book Fair. Volunteers from the Asterford University English Society read stories aloud every hour, and young visitors can exchange a book they have finished for one brought by another child.

On weekdays the Student Health Centre at Asterford University is open from 08:00 to 19:00, with appointments available throughout the day. Students can see a doctor, a nurse or a pharmacist, and the centre also runs clinics for travel vaccinations, sports injuries and sexual health.

The Asterford University campus is divided by the River Wend into two parts. The older south bank holds the original college buildings, the Rose Quadrangle and the main libraries, while the newer north bank contains the science buildings, most of the residences and the sports facilities.

The Brannock Hills surround Asterford on three sides and are crossed by a network of footpaths and old drovers' roads. On clear days walkers on the highest ridge can see the distant coast, and the hills are popular with students for weekend hikes, picnics and cross-country runs.

The Ridgeway Sports Centre is the main sports facility of Asterford University and stands on a hillside above the residences. It includes a large sports hall, a fitness suite, squash courts and an indoor climbing wall, and it is open to members of the public at off-peak times for a small fee.

The Photography Club has its own darkroom in the basement of the Student Union, where members develop black and white film by hand. The club organises photo walks around the old town and the riverbank, and an exhibition of members' best pictures is held in the Student Union hall each summer.

The university arboretum covers a gentle slope on the western side of the campus and contains trees from many parts of the world. Its collection of oaks and maples is especially colourful in autumn, and a marked trail with information boards leads visitors through the different sections.

On Shrove Tuesday students from each residence race through the market square carrying frying pans and tossing pancakes as they run. The pancake race is said to have started as a challenge between two rival residences, and the winning team is rewarded with free breakfasts at Juniper Refectory for a week.

Aster Archive was carefully renovated in 1978, when new climate controls, fire doors and steel shelving were installed in the strong rooms. During the renovation the collections were moved temporarily to the basement of Hollin Library, and readers had to request documents a day in advance until the work was finished.

Kestrel Boathouse, the home of the Asterford University Boat Club, is built from cedar. The timber was chosen because it resists rot in the damp air beside the River Wend, and the warm reddish walls of the boathouse have become a familiar sight for walkers and joggers on the towpath.

Each summer a traditional river blessing takes place on the River Wend, when the university chaplain and the mayor of Asterford ride in a decorated boat from the old stone bridge to the mill weir. The ceremony dates back to the days when the mills depended on the river for their power.

The university tennis courts lie behind Juniper Refectory and are surrounded by tall hedges that shelter players from the wind. The courts can be booked by any student, and in summer the tennis club holds an open tournament that ends with a strawberry tea for players and spectators.

Asterford General Hospital serves the town and the surrounding valley and works closely with the medical school of the university. It has an emergency department, a maternity unit and several specialist wards, and many of its doctors also teach students on clinical placements.

Each spring the crews of Kestrel Boathouse race against Dunmere College in a long-standing contest on the River Wend. The race covers about two kilometres between the old stone bridge and the mill weir, and the winning crew keeps a silver oar until the following year.

Asterford is a market town of about thirty-one thousand people set in a broad valley among the Brannock Hills. The university is the largest employer in the town, and during term time students make up a large share of the people seen in its streets, cafes and shops.

The medical school of Asterford University trains doctors in partnership with Asterford General Hospital. Students spend their early years studying anatomy, physiology and clinical skills on campus, then move into hospital wards and community clinics across the region for the later part of their training.

The Green Kettle is a small vegetarian cafe on Tanner Street run by a cooperative of former students. It serves soups, salads and homemade cakes at modest prices, hosts poetry readings on the first Monday of each month, and keeps a shelf of board games for customers who wish to stay a while.

The Careers Service of Asterford University helps students prepare for life after their studies. Advisers offer individual meetings, practice interviews and help with writing applications, and the service organises a large careers fair each winter where employers from the region meet students looking for jobs and internships.

Since 2019 the Campus Loop shuttle has used quiet electric buses painted in deep green and silver, the colours of Asterford University. The buses are charged overnight at a depot on Mill Road, and each one has space for two wheelchairs and several bicycles.

The Sable Chemistry Laboratory has 52 fume cupboards, which remove harmful vapours while students carry out experiments. The cupboards are arranged in long rows across two teaching rooms, and each one is tested every term by the laboratory technicians to make sure that the air flow is strong enough for safe work.

Every new student at Asterford University is paired with an older student mentor from the same course. Mentors meet their new students during the first weeks of term, show them around the campus and answer questions about lectures, assignments and life in the town.

The Gardening Club looks after a set of allotments on the southern edge of the campus, where members grow potatoes, beans, herbs and soft fruit. Surplus produce is sold at a stall outside Juniper Refectory, and the money raised is used to buy seeds and tools for the next season.

Pellam Observatory was built in 1911 on Signal Hill, the highest point of the Asterford University grounds. It is named after Lady Honora Pellam, a keen amateur astronomer who paid for the building and left her own collection of star charts and instruments to the university.

Pages and Pens is an independent bookshop on Tanner Street that has served Asterford for many decades. Its narrow rooms are packed from floor to ceiling with new and second-hand books, and the owners keep a table of recommended titles chosen by students and staff of the university.

The Marrow Physics Laboratory is located in Calder House, a three-storey brick building beside the eastern car park of Asterford University. The ground floor of Calder House holds the laboratory's workshops and vibration-free rooms, while the upper floors contain offices, a seminar room and a small library of physics journals.

The Winter Book Fair lasts four days and attracts book lovers from across the region to Asterford. Each day of the fair has its own theme, such as poetry, local history or children's books, and the organisers arrange readings by visiting authors in the evenings.

Several departments at Asterford University keep their own small libraries for specialist books and journals. These departmental libraries are usually staffed by volunteers or part-time assistants, and they offer quiet study spaces close to the lecture rooms used by each subject.

Hobbs Bakery on Mill Road has supplied bread to Asterford for more than a century and is a favourite stop for students on their way to lectures. It is best known for its cheese and onion rolls and for a dark rye loaf made to a recipe brought to the town by the founder's grandmother.

On Thursday evenings in summer a night market of food stalls fills the lane behind the Student Union. Stallholders from the town and from student societies sell dumplings, curries, pancakes and grilled vegetables, and the market has become a popular place to meet friends after classes.

The Rose Quadrangle is the oldest courtyard of Asterford University and is surrounded by the original college buildings of the nineteenth century. Its central lawn is bordered by beds of old-fashioned roses that bloom in early summer, and graduating students traditionally have their photographs taken beside the stone sundial in its centre.

The Cycling Club organises group rides along the quiet lanes around Asterford, ranging from gentle trips to nearby villages to demanding climbs over the Brannock Hills. Members share tips on bicycle maintenance, and the club runs a free repair session in the Student Union courtyard once a fortnight.

The Corn Exchange was built in the nineteenth century when Asterford was one of the busiest grain markets in the region. After the trade declined, the building stood empty for many years until the university bought and restored it to serve as the home of the Student Union.

The Varden Gardens, named after the founder of Asterford University, include a tall glasshouse built in the nineteenth century and filled with tropical plants. The glasshouse is kept warm throughout the year, and visitors can see banana plants, orchids and a giant water lily whose leaves are strong enough to support a small child.

Brannock blue cheese has been made on farms around Asterford for generations. It is a soft, crumbly cheese with blue veins, aged in cool stone cellars, and it is served at many formal university dinners alongside oatcakes and chutney made from local apples.

Rugby is one of the most popular sports at Asterford University, and the first team plays its home matches on the main pitch beside the Ridgeway Sports Centre. Matches against neighbouring universities often draw large crowds of students, who sing and cheer from the grassy bank above the pitch.

Hollin Library opened in 1888 and was named after Thomas Hollin, a wool merchant who left his fortune to Asterford University for the purchase of books. His portrait still hangs above the main staircase, and a small plaque by the entrance records the date on which the library first welcomed readers.

The Founders' Lantern Walk was first held in 1892, fifty years after the founding of Asterford University in 1842. The early walks were small gatherings of students and teachers, but the event grew steadily and today it attracts several thousand people, including many families from the town.

The Asterford Alumni Association keeps former students in touch with the university and with each other. It publishes a magazine twice a year, organises reunions on campus every summer, and supports current students through mentoring schemes and donations to the hardship fund.

Graduates of Asterford University wear black gowns with hoods lined in deep green silk, the colour of the university. Each degree is marked by a different trim on the hood, and the gowns are hired from a family firm in the town that has supplied academic dress for over a century.

The law school of Asterford University is known for its moot court, a room designed to look like a real courtroom where students argue imaginary cases before visiting judges. The school also runs a free legal advice clinic for residents of the town, supervised by qualified lawyers.

The herb garden behind the medical school was planted to teach students about plants used in traditional medicine. Neat beds of lavender, sage, foxglove and camomile are labelled with their Latin names, and a small pavilion at the end of the garden is used for outdoor classes in fine weather.

Trains run from Asterford to the city of Carrowmouth roughly once an hour, and the journey takes about forty minutes. Many students travel to Carrowmouth at weekends for shopping, concerts and football matches, and some members of staff commute from the city every day.

The box office of Tamsin Arts Centre opens at 11:00 each day, when staff begin selling tickets for concerts, plays and film screenings. Students of Asterford University can buy reduced-price tickets at the box office counter by showing their student card, and the most popular performances often sell out within the first hour.

Josiah Varden, the banker who founded Asterford University, made his fortune lending money to the mills along the River Wend. He believed that a university would keep talented young people in the region, and he gave the land for the first college buildings as well as a sum of money to pay the early professors.

The Winter Book Fair was first organised in 1967 by a group of students who wanted to raise money for Hollin Library. It now brings together around sixty booksellers from across the region, and part of the money raised each year is still given to the library for new books.

Brindle Hall houses 214 students in single and shared rooms arranged around a central courtyard. Most residents are in their first year at Asterford University, and each corridor has a shared kitchen, a common room and a senior student who helps new arrivals settle in during their first weeks on campus.

Women were first admitted to Asterford University in 1879, after a long campaign led by a group of teachers from the town. The first women students attended lectures alongside men but lived in a separate house near the market square, and within ten years they made up almost a third of the student body.

The Varden Lecture Theatre is the largest lecture hall at Asterford University, with steeply raked wooden seating that curves around a central stage. It is used for first-year lectures, public talks and debates, and its excellent acoustics mean that speakers rarely need a microphone.

The swimming pool at the Ridgeway Sports Centre is twenty-five metres long and has six lanes. Early morning sessions are reserved for lane swimming, while afternoons are given over to lessons and club training, and the university water polo team practises there on weekday evenings.

Snow falls in Asterford only a few times each winter, usually in January or February. When it does, students build snowmen on the lawns in front of the main buildings, and a friendly snowball fight between the residences has become an informal tradition after the first heavy fall.

Professor Desmond Achterberg was born in the coastal town of Harwick and studied at the city university of Carrowmouth before beginning his career. He is a keen chess player and has captained the staff team in the annual match between lecturers and the Asterford University Chess Club.

Besides its main telescope, Pellam Observatory has a historic refracting telescope with a lens of 30 centimetres, which was the first instrument installed in the building. The white-painted dome rotates on iron wheels and was restored by a team of engineering students and volunteers from the town astronomy society.

The market square lies at the heart of Asterford and has hosted a weekly market every Wednesday for several centuries. Stalls sell vegetables, cheese, bread, flowers and second-hand clothes, and many students buy their weekly groceries there because the prices are lower than in the supermarkets.

The Wend Weekly is the student newspaper of Asterford University and is written and edited entirely by volunteers. It is published every Friday during term and covers campus news, reviews of concerts and plays, sports results and opinion columns, and many of its former editors have gone on to careers in journalism.

The Department of Maritime History occupies the top floor of Harbour House on the western edge of the Asterford University campus. Its corridors are lined with paintings of sailing ships, and a reading room holds copies of harbour records, ship logs and sea charts used by students in their research.

The Asterford Courier is the town's weekly newspaper and has been published since the middle of the nineteenth century. It reports on local council decisions, sport, farming and university news, and its letters page is well known for lively arguments between students and long-standing residents.

The Volunteering Society connects students with local charities in Asterford, including a food bank, an animal shelter and a reading scheme for primary school children. Volunteers give a few hours each week, and the society estimates that its members contribute thousands of hours to the town every year.

A coat of arms was granted to Asterford University soon after its foundation and shows an open book above a silver star on a deep green shield. The star refers to the name of the town, while the book represents learning, and the design appears on the university seal, degree certificates and the gates of the main entrance.

The university chapel was built in the nineteenth century and stands at the eastern end of the Rose Quadrangle. It is used for services, concerts and quiet reflection, and the chaplaincy team supports students of all faiths and none through conversation, community meals and a small prayer room.

The Campus Loop shuttle starts at Wendgate Station, the small railway station on the eastern side of Asterford. From the station the electric buses travel past the Student Union, the science buildings and the residences before returning, so passengers arriving by train can reach the campus without a long walk.

The old mills along the River Wend closed during the last century as the wool trade declined. Several of the mill buildings have since been converted into flats, workshops and offices, and one of them now houses the studios of the university's fine art students.

The Department of Music occupies a modern building beside the Varden Gardens with practice rooms, a recording studio and a recital hall. Students study composition, performance and music history, and lunchtime recitals given by students and staff are free and open to the public every week of term.

The Sable Chemistry Laboratory opened in 1958 and is named after Edith Sable, a chemist who studied natural dyes extracted from plants. The main teaching rooms can hold about one hundred and twenty students at a time, and the laboratory is used for practical classes by chemistry, biology and medicine students.

Professor Orla Penhaligon joined Asterford University in 2009 after leading research expeditions to remote northern ice fields. She has her office in the Department of Earth Sciences, where a large photograph of her first field camp hangs on the wall beside a map of the places she has studied.

The Department of Art History has a small gallery that displays prints, drawings and paintings donated to Asterford University over the past century. Students on the curating course plan and install one exhibition each year, writing the labels and catalogue themselves.

Professor Orla Penhaligon won the Selwick Medal for her research on the history of the northern ice fields. The award is given every two years to a scientist whose field work has changed the understanding of a cold region, and Professor Penhaligon was the first member of Asterford University staff to receive it.

The lanterns carried in the Founders' Lantern Walk are made by hand in workshops held at the Student Union during the weeks before the event. Most are paper globes in the university colours of deep green and silver, and prizes are given for the most imaginative designs.

The old stone bridge over the River Wend has five arches and was built in the fifteenth century to carry the main road into Asterford. Heavy vehicles have been banned from the bridge for many years, and it is now used only by pedestrians, cyclists and the occasional horse.

The chief technician of the Sable Chemistry Laboratory is Rufus Dellacourt, who has worked at Asterford University for over twenty years. He is responsible for ordering chemicals, maintaining the equipment and training new students in safe working practices during their first practical class.

The Midsummer Picnic is an informal tradition at Asterford University, held on the lawns of the Varden Gardens on the longest evening of the year. Students bring blankets, food and musical instruments, and the picnic usually continues until the sun finally sets behind the Brannock Hills.

The dome of Tamsin Arts Centre is turquoise, and it can be seen from most parts of Asterford because the building stands on a small rise above the market square. The colour comes from glazed tiles that were fitted when the centre opened, and local people often use the dome as a landmark when giving directions.

The Student Union of Asterford University is based in the old Corn Exchange, a grand stone hall on the edge of the market square that once hosted the town's grain trade. Today it contains a bar, a cafe, meeting rooms for clubs and societies, and a large hall used for concerts and dances.

On Saturdays Aster Archive is open from 10:00 until 13:00 for a short morning session, and the building stays closed on Sundays and public holidays. The Saturday session is popular with townspeople researching their family history, and an archivist is always on duty to help visitors read old handwriting.

New students at Asterford University are formally welcomed at the matriculation ceremony held in the first week of the academic year. Wearing short black gowns, they gather in the Rose Quadrangle for a group photograph and then listen to a speech by the vice-chancellor about the history and values of the university.

The International Students Society welcomes students from more than seventy countries who study at Asterford University. It runs a buddy scheme for newcomers, organises trips to nearby cities and holds a large festival of food and music every spring in the Student Union hall.

The Founders' Lantern Walk ends at Quarry Green, a wide lawn on the edge of the campus that was once a stone quarry. When the last walkers arrive, the lanterns are placed together in a large circle on Quarry Green and the university choir sings a short programme before the crowd slowly returns home.

Professor Desmond Achterberg is a professor of economics at Asterford University who specialises in the history of banking. He teaches the first-year course on money and markets, which is known for its lively lectures, and he served for six years as dean of the Faculty of Social Sciences.

Summers in Asterford are generally warm and pleasant, and many students spend the long evenings on the riverbank or in the university gardens. Heat waves are rare, but when they occur the town council turns on the outdoor fountain in the market square so that children can cool down.

St Brannoc's Church stands on the north side of the market square and is the oldest building in Asterford. Its square stone tower was built in the twelfth century, and its bells ring out across the town on Sunday mornings and on special occasions such as graduation day.

On weekdays the Campus Loop shuttle runs every 12 minutes, linking the main teaching buildings of Asterford University with the residences and the town centre. The frequent service means that most students do not need to check a timetable, and drivers keep to the schedule by using a dedicated bus lane on Mill Road.

Juniper Refectory is the largest dining hall at Asterford University and serves breakfast, lunch and dinner throughout the term. Meals are cooked on site using vegetables from local farms, and long wooden tables beneath its high windows give the refectory the feel of a traditional college hall.

Examinations at Asterford University are held mainly in the summer term in large halls across the campus. Students sit at individual desks in long rows, and invigilators walk between them to check that the rules are followed and to help anyone who feels unwell during a paper.

Laundry rooms with washing machines and dryers are provided in every residence at Asterford University. The machines are operated with a card that students top up online, and a laundry rota helps to prevent long queues on Sunday evenings, which are traditionally the busiest time.

Winters in Asterford are usually mild but wet, with long periods of drizzle carried in from the west. The cobbled streets of the old town become slippery in the rain, and the university spreads grit on the steeper paths of the campus during cold spells to prevent falls.

The academic year at Asterford University is divided into three terms named autumn, spring and summer. Teaching takes place mainly in the first two terms, while the summer term is devoted largely to revision, examinations and the many concerts, sports events and celebrations that follow them.

Research at the Marrow Physics Laboratory focuses on low-temperature physics. The laboratory operates several cryostats that cool samples to within a few degrees of absolute zero, and it supplies liquid helium to other science groups at Asterford University through a recycling system installed in its basement.

The Asterford Science Park was opened by the university on the eastern edge of the town to help young companies grow from university research. It now houses small firms working on medical devices, clean energy and software, and many of them employ graduates of the university.

Early mornings in Asterford are often foggy, especially in autumn, when cool air settles in the valley and mist rises from the River Wend. Students walking to early lectures sometimes cannot see the far side of the quadrangle, although the fog usually lifts by the middle of the morning.

The Disability Support Service helps students with physical disabilities, learning differences and long-term health conditions to take a full part in university life. It arranges extra time in examinations, provides specialist equipment and software, and works with departments to make teaching materials accessible.

The Marrow Physics Laboratory is directed by Professor Anselm Grieve, who joined the laboratory after many years of research abroad. The laboratory welcomes school groups on open days, when visitors can watch a magnet float above a cooled superconductor and talk to doctoral students about their experiments.

Aster Archive was completed in 1906, after four years of building work paid for by a gift from the town council and a group of former students. The grey limestone building was designed to protect the university's charters, letters and account books from damp, and its thick walls still keep the strong rooms cool throughout the summer.

The Campus Loop shuttle is free for all students and staff of Asterford University, who simply show their university card when they board. The service is paid for by the university and the town council together, and townspeople can also use it for a small fare.

The Department of Computer Science moved into a new glass-fronted building in the science park in the early years of this century. Its research groups work on artificial intelligence, computer security and software for medicine, and students take part in an annual programming contest held over a weekend.

The Asterford University Orchestra has around sixty players, most of them students from departments other than music. It rehearses on Monday evenings and performs three major concerts each year, including a winter concert in St Brannoc's Church that usually sells out weeks in advance.

The Student Health Centre offers free counselling to all students at Asterford University. A team of five counsellors provides short courses of individual sessions, group workshops on exam stress and sleep, and a weekly drop-in hour for students who simply want to talk to someone.

The Hiking Club of Asterford University leads walks into the Brannock Hills almost every Sunday during term. Routes are graded by difficulty, and experienced members teach newcomers how to read maps, choose suitable clothing and plan for sudden changes in the weather on the exposed ridges.

The university hardship fund provides emergency grants to students who face unexpected financial difficulties, such as a broken laptop, a family crisis or a sudden rise in rent. Applications are assessed quickly by a small committee, and the fund is supported by donations from former students and staff.

Early in the twentieth century a great flood of the River Wend damaged several university buildings near the water. Students and townspeople worked together to rescue books and furniture from the ground floors, and a stone marker beside the old bridge still shows how high the water rose.

The route of the Founders' Lantern Walk is about three kilometres long and takes roughly an hour and a half to complete at a slow pace. Volunteer stewards in green sashes guide the crowd at each corner, and the town council closes several streets to traffic for the evening.

The vice-chancellor of Asterford University is Professor Helen Ashdown, a chemist who previously led a research institute in Carrowmouth. Since taking office she has focused on improving student housing, expanding research partnerships with local industry and reducing the university's energy use.

Foxes, badgers and owls are regularly seen on the Asterford University campus, especially around the arboretum and the allotments. A student wildlife group records sightings each year, and bird boxes fixed to trees across the campus provide nesting places for tits, robins and woodpeckers.

The Department of Modern Languages teaches French, German, Spanish, Italian and several other languages to students across Asterford University. Students on language degrees spend their third year abroad, and the department's conversation cafe gives everyone a chance to practise speaking with native speakers over tea.

Car parking on the Asterford University campus is limited, and permits are given mainly to staff and to students with disabilities. The university promotes walking, cycling and the use of public transport, and most visitors use the public car park near the market square.

Professor Orla Penhaligon has published more than eighty scientific papers and supervises a group of doctoral students who study ice, climate and sea level. Her group spends several weeks each year at field stations in cold regions, collecting samples that are later analysed in the freezer laboratories at Asterford University.

The Student Health Centre closes at 12:30 on Saturdays and does not open on Sundays. Outside these hours, students who need medical help can contact the town's out-of-hours service or go to Asterford General Hospital, which has an emergency department about two kilometres from the campus.

Professor Desmond Achterberg wrote The Quiet Ledger, a book that tells the story of small family banks in the hill towns and how they survived periods of crisis. The book was praised for its readable style and is now set as background reading for several economics courses at Asterford University.

The Department of Maritime History was founded in 1923, when Asterford University received a large collection of ship logs and harbour records from a shipping family. The department began with two lecturers and a handful of students, who studied the collection in a single room above a warehouse near the river.

Brindle Hall is a student residence at Asterford University that is easy to recognise from the street because its front door is painted scarlet. The bright door was chosen by the first residents and has been repainted in the same colour ever since, so visitors are often told simply to look for the scarlet door on Larch Lane.

The Film Society screens classic and foreign films every Wednesday evening in a lecture theatre fitted with a proper projection screen. Each screening is introduced by a member who explains the background of the film, and the society publishes a printed programme of its films at the start of every term.

The Department of Geography runs field courses in the Brannock Hills, where students study river erosion, soils and changes in land use. Its map library holds old survey maps of the valley, which show how the town of Asterford grew from a cluster of houses beside the river into a busy market town.

Professor Desmond Achterberg joined Asterford University in 1994 as a young lecturer in economics. He arrived from a post at a research institute and quickly became known for his clear teaching, and within a few years he had set up the university's first seminar series on the history of banking and public debt.

The bells of the university chapel are rung by a team of student bell ringers on Sunday mornings and before major ceremonies. Bell ringing at Asterford follows an old tradition of change ringing, in which the bells are rung in changing patterns, and new ringers practise for months before joining a performance.

The Regal is the only cinema in Asterford and occupies a grand building from the early twentieth century on Mill Road. It shows new releases alongside older films, offers discounted tickets to students on Monday evenings, and still has its original decorated ceiling and velvet curtains.

Students working in the Sable Chemistry Laboratory wear amber lab coats. The bright colour was introduced so that laboratory staff can quickly tell students apart from technicians, who wear white, and so that anyone leaving the laboratory while still wearing a coat is easily noticed at the door.

Campus security staff patrol the grounds of Asterford University day and night and can be called on to escort students home after dark. Their office is near the main gate, and they also manage lost property, parking permits and the emergency alarm system across the campus.

The current head librarian of Hollin Library is Bernard Quill, who has led the library since 2016. Under his direction the library has digitised much of its local history collection, introduced self-service machines for borrowing and returning books, and opened a new space for students who need help with academic writing.

Every autumn the Student Health Centre runs free flu vaccination clinics for students and staff, held in the Student Union over several afternoons. The centre also registers new students with a doctor during their first week, and nurses visit the residences to answer questions about staying healthy at university.

The upper floor of Kestrel Boathouse contains a training room with rowing machines and weights, a changing room and a small clubroom with a balcony overlooking the river. Trophies won by the Asterford University Boat Club are displayed in a long glass cabinet in the clubroom.

On Saturdays and Sundays the Campus Loop shuttle runs every 20 minutes, because fewer students travel to lectures at the weekend. The weekend timetable starts later in the morning, and the last bus of the evening leaves the Student Union shortly before midnight.

The university mailroom sorts thousands of letters and parcels every day for students, staff and departments. Students living in residences collect their post from pigeonholes in the entrance hall of each building, and larger parcels are held at a collection point in the Student Union.

The Department of Maritime History at Asterford University is headed by Professor Ilse Marquand, a specialist in the trade routes of northern harbours. Since taking charge she has expanded the department's oral history project, which records interviews with retired sailors, dock workers and shipbuilders from the coastal towns downstream from Asterford.

The Winter Book Fair of Asterford University is held in Greymantle Hall, a large timber-roofed hall that is normally used for examinations and formal dinners. During the fair, the long tables of Greymantle Hall are covered with second-hand books, rare editions and maps, and the gallery above is turned into a reading area.

Asterford University offers a range of scholarships for students from families with low incomes, including the Varden Scholarship, which covers accommodation costs for the full length of a degree. Scholarships are funded by gifts from former students and by the income of the founder's original endowment.
